source.author: lucan
source.text: Mox cetera cantu Explicat Haemonio, penetratque in Tartara lingua: Eumenides, Stygiumque nefas, poenaeque nocentum: Et Chaos innumeros avidum confundere mundos: Et rector terrae, quem longa in saecula torquet Mors dilata deum: Styx, et, quos nulla meretur Thessalis Elysios: coelum matremque perosa Persephone, nostraeque Hecates pars ultima, per quam Manibus et mihi sunt tacitae commercia linguae: Ianitor et sedis laxae, qui viscera saevo Spargis nostra cani: repetitaque fila sorores Tracturae: tuque o flagrantis portitor undae, Iam lassate senex ad me redeuntibus umbris: Exaudite preces, si vos satis ore nefando Pollutoque voco, si numquam haec carmina fibris Humanis ieiuna cano, si pectora plena Saepe dedi, et lavi calido prosecta cerebro; Si quis, cum vestris caput extaque lancibus, infans, Imposui, victurus erat: parete precanti.
source.text_original: Mox cetera cantu / Explicat Haemonio, penetratque in Tartara lingua: / Eumenides, Stygiumque nefas, poenaeque nocentum: / Et Chaos innumeros avidum confundere mundos: / Et rector terrae, quem longa in saecula torquet / Mors dilata deum: Styx, et, quos nulla meretur / Thessalis Elysios: coelum matremque perosa / Persephone, nostraeque Hecates pars ultima, per quam / Manibus et mihi sunt tacitae commercia linguae: / Ianitor et sedis laxae, qui viscera saevo / Spargis nostra cani: repetitaque fila sorores / Tracturae: tuque o flagrantis portitor undae, / Iam lassate senex ad me redeuntibus umbris: / Exaudite preces, si vos satis ore nefando / Pollutoque voco, si numquam haec carmina fibris / Humanis ieiuna cano, si pectora plena / Saepe dedi, et lavi calido prosecta cerebro; / Si quis, cum vestris caput extaque lancibus, infans, / Imposui, victurus erat: parete precanti.
source.text_english: Soon he unfolds the rest in Haemonian song and forces his way with his speech into Tartarus: the Eumenides, and the Stygian crime, and the punishments of the guilty; and Chaos, greedy to confuse countless worlds; and the ruler of the earth, whom delayed death torments through long ages as a god; Styx, and the Elysiums undeserved by Thessalian hands; Persephone, hating heaven and her mother, and the farthest part of our Hecate, through whom the tongue of silence gives me access to the Shades: and the doorkeeper of the open hall, who with savage watchfulness scatters our limbs to the dog; and the sisters who are to draw the spun threads again; and you too, ferryman of the blazing stream, now weary old man, when the Shades are returning to me: hear my prayers, if I call you enough with impious and polluted mouth, if never with hungry lips do I sing these spells, if I have often given you full breasts, and washed the severed flesh in warm bloodless brains; if any child, with his head and entrails in your bowls, was meant to live, when I placed them there: obey the suppliant.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: Cardine sub nostro rebusque abscissa supernis Tartarei sedet aula patris, non illa ruenti accessura polo, victam si volvere molem ingenti iacet ore Chaos, quod pondere fessam materiem lapsumque queat consumere mundum.
reuse.text_original: Cardine sub nostro rebusque abscissa supernis / Tartarei sedet aula patris, non illa ruenti / accessura polo, victam si volvere molem / ingenti †iacet ore Chaos, quod pondere fessam / materiem lapsumque queat consumere mundum.
reuse.text_english: Beneath our pole and cut off from the things above sits the court of the Tartarean father, not one that would join itself to the falling sky, if Chaos, lying with its vast jaws, should be able to swallow up the mass once conquered, and consume the world as it sinks, weighed down by its burden.
